video.title: The Most Profitable Side Hustle You've Never Heard Of

summary: Chris Koerner interviews the owners of The Social Greenhouse, a Dallas plant bingo event business. They describe validating the idea through TikTok, testing it at their own venue, and growing through ticket presales and venue partners that share their content. They report early revenue and profit figures, while noting that the work includes buying and transporting plants and running live events. The model may transfer to other themes or cities, but the transcript leaves ticketing systems, staffing needs at scale, and the economics of helping other operators unspecified.

ideas.name: Plant bingo events
ideas.one_liner: Run ticketed bingo nights at breweries and other venues, with plants as prizes and the venue sharing promotion.
ideas.business_model: Sell event tickets and additional bingo boards; venues provide space without a fee and benefit from attendees buying food and drinks.
ideas.customer: Attendees looking for a social activity, including groups on date nights or girls' nights; the owners say most attendees are women aged 25 to 55, and relatively few are plant enthusiasts. Venue partners are also customers or collaborators.
ideas.problem: People want a fun activity and a reason to visit a venue; venues want customers on quieter nights.
ideas.offer: A hosted bingo event with plants as prizes. The standard ticket includes bingo boards for multiple rounds; attendees can buy extra boards. Some events may use a theme such as mystery plants.

pricing.model: Per-person event ticket, with additional bingo boards sold at the event.

price_points.label: Venue fee in the described arrangement

pricing.notes: Extra bingo boards are sold, but their price is not stated. The first event included free pizza; later food and drinks were left to the venue.

acquisition_channels.details: The owners posted TikTok and Instagram videos, initially through personal accounts and later with footage from events. They say views on TikTok correlated with ticket sales.

quote.text: So to find customers, post organically to Instagram and Tik Tok. You don't have to have a ton of followers.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

acquisition_channels.details: They partnered with breweries and other venues, using quieter nights. The venues shared event content with their own audiences; the owners handled the event work and marketing.

quote.text: So already from the start we're getting a big reach. The piggyback the classic piggyback.
quote.speaker: Guest (name not stated)

acquisition_channels.details: The guest recommends reaching out to local plant Facebook groups, which they describe as tight-knit communities. The transcript does not say this was a channel they had already used to sell tickets.

quote.text: there's so many different Facebook groups for plants in literally every single town, city, and they're tight-knit communities.
quote.speaker: Guest (name not stated)

acquisition_channels.details: They made Facebook Events for their events. The transcript does not name a ticketing platform.
Chris recommends calling restaurant, brewery, and event venue owners to pitch the event. In the UK, business calls should screen against applicable TPS/CTPS preferences.

quote.text: Pick up the phone and call a restaurant owner, brewery owner, events owner, chicken and pickle, pickle ball, like anywhere that hosts people of at least 50 people.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

ideas.delivery: The owners buy and transport plants, prepare bingo boards and supplies, set up at the venue, host the rounds, and take down equipment. They sometimes hire hosts to help; the owners have also run events themselves. The venue provides seating and may already have speakers and a microphone.
unit_economics_claims: The first event had 25 attendees paying $10 each and included a free plant; the guest said the business lost money on it.
The owners estimate plants average $10 to $12 per attendee, with a mix of lower- and higher-priced plants.
They report a 50-person event can sell about 30 extra bingo boards.
They report a recent 150-person event brought in about $5,300, including about $500 from extra bingo boards, and they took home about $3,000 after paying two hosts $200 each.
They report February revenue of about $21,000 and project March revenue of about $25,000; they say costs were initially mostly plants and supplies.
The guest says events are typically around 75 attendees and that take-home profit can be at least 50%, depending on staffing and event costs.
ideas.startup_cost: The guest says the business could be started without money by preselling an event, but their own initial purchases included a speaker, microphone, bingo boards, dobbers, plants, a fold-up table, and stickers. They describe the initial equipment and plant spend as a few hundred dollars.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Not stated. They sold event tickets weeks or months before event dates; the first event was their initial test.

acquisition.how: Agents could help prepare and schedule social posts, monitor inbound interest, and draft venue pitches. People still need to create event content and establish venue partnerships; the guest's suggested phone outreach requires human calls and UK preference screening.

onboarding.how: A ticketing form could collect attendee details and send event information, but the transcript does not state what they use or how they handle attendee questions and changes.

delivery.how: A human must source, transport, and set up plants and supplies and host the live event. The physical work caps delivery automation.

billing.how: Presales show that payment is collected before events, but the payment platform and reconciliation process are not stated. Payment processing could be automated, with human checks for walk-ins and extra boards.

support.how: Attendees may need live help during the event, and the owners or hosts are present to run it. Automated answers could handle routine pre-event questions.

uk_applicability.notes: The event and venue-partnership model can work in the UK. Local demand, venue economics, plant sourcing, and any rules for selling plants would need checking. The Texas plant licensing comment is specific to the guest's location. Venue outreach by phone should respect UK TPS/CTPS rules.

risks: The first test event lost money, and plants are a material per-attendee cost.
The model depends on venues sharing promotion and on attendees turning up; the guest says they have no-shows and sometimes oversell or accept walk-ins.
Buying, transporting, setting up, and storing plants and event supplies creates physical work and limits unattended operation.
The guest says a license is required to sell plants in Texas; UK requirements should be checked locally before selling plants.
Reported event margins may fall as they hire hosts; the guest says staffing reduces the margin.
The host's estimate of roughly $30,000 profit in the first two months is not reconciled with the guest's stated monthly revenue figures.

tactics.name: Validate visible demand before committing
steps: Notice an event concept on TikTok and check the original operator's account and website.
Look for evidence of demand such as high-view videos and sold-out scheduled events.
Compare the concept with existing bingo or trivia nights that already draw people.

quote.text: I checked their website and they had 10 events next month and half of them were sold out already.
quote.speaker: Guest (name not stated)

tactics.name: Run a small test event at a venue you control
steps: Use an existing venue to test logistics and audience response.
Charge a low introductory ticket price and include a simple extra such as food.
Treat the first event as a test of setup, hosting, and customer reactions, even if it loses money.

quote.text: Yeah. It was like, okay, let's see if this actually can work. Let's see how the logistics work. Let's make sure Steph's comfortable.
quote.speaker: Guest (name not stated)

tactics.name: Piggyback on venue promotion
steps: Approach venues that already host trivia or bingo and have enough seating.
Offer an event on a quieter night so the venue can earn from food and drink sales.
Agree a no-fee arrangement in which the event operators handle the work and marketing.
Ask the venue to share event content with its existing audience.

quote.text: We do all the work. We market it and then we just hopefully they want to share it with their people, but otherwise we collect the money.
quote.speaker: Guest (name not stated)

tactics.name: Use organic social posts and community groups
steps: Post short event videos organically on TikTok and Instagram.
Use personal accounts to seed early reach, then make content from actual events.
Create Facebook Events for each date.
Reach out to local plant groups with an event that supports the community rather than only advertising the business.

quote.text: And just do videos. Tik Tok, Instagram has worked amazingly well for us.
quote.speaker: Guest (name not stated)

tactics.name: Presell dates and use extra boards to increase event revenue
steps: List event dates weeks or months ahead and collect ticket revenue before buying event supplies.
Offer additional bingo boards at the event; the guest reports selling around 30 extra boards at a 50-person event.
Use observed no-shows to decide whether to allow a limited number of oversold tickets or walk-ins.

quote.text: And the events sell you know weeks months in advance which is great for our cash flow.
quote.speaker: Guest (name not stated)

tactics.name: Keep the initial kit small and use venue equipment
steps: Buy only the core supplies needed for the event, including plants and printed bingo materials.
Ask whether the venue already has a speaker and microphone before buying more equipment.
Use an existing venue or host at home to avoid venue hire costs.

quote.text: And even like half the venues we go to have speakers and microphone there to do trivia. You just buy plants and print some papers.
quote.speaker: Guest (name not stated)

tactics.name: Use hosts to reduce event-day pressure
steps: Run early events yourselves while learning setup and venue logistics.
Hire hosts to help run events when the workload or event size makes it worthwhile.
Compare the reduction in stress with the lower profit after host pay.

quote.text: So, like I don't mind making a little bit less to make it easier.
quote.speaker: Guest (name not stated)

warnings.warning: The guest says a license is required to sell plants in Texas. Confirm the applicable local rules before selling plants in another jurisdiction.
The first event was intentionally priced cheaply and lost money; it was a validation test, not evidence of profitable unit economics.
The host's claim of $30,000 profit in the first two months is not reconciled with the guest's reported January and February revenue figures.
Overselling relies on estimates of no-shows and can create capacity and customer-service problems if too many attendees arrive.
The host included a sponsor read endorsing Bizzy, an incorporation service. This is a promotional conflict in the video.

evidence_quality.rationale: The operators describe their own process and provide several specific early revenue, cost, attendance, and event details. The business is only a few months old in the account, the transcript has ambiguous speaker attribution and some rough or conflicting figures, and the host's $30,000 profit framing is not supported by the guest's monthly revenue figures.
evidence_quality.promotional_conflict: The host reads an endorsement for Bizzy, an incorporation service, with a call to visit its website.
